description: Finger hangs build the strongest cables in the hand, and done wrong they wreck the pulleys that guide them. Here are the five mistakes that destroy finger pulleys, the test that tells you if you are even ready, and the safe way to earn this exercise.

lines: If the warm-up hurts, stop. That is data.
beats.title: THE READINESS TEST

beats.text: FEET LIGHT, NOT FEET OFF, AT FIRST

scenes.narration: Find a ledge | you can trust: | a doorframe top, | a stair edge, | a thick branch. | Fingers on top, | pads gripping down, | no thumb at all. | Now take weight | onto your fingers | slowly, feet still down, | until you feel | real tension. | Then, only if | nothing hurts, | lift one foot. | Time your hold | with control. | This test grades | your finger cables | and your pulleys together. | Any sharp pain | in a finger joint | ends the test | immediately, full stop. | Got your TIME? | Keep it. | At the end, | I grade the pulleys.

lines: Under 10 means build the base first.
beats.title: THE READINESS LINE

scenes.label: CONTROLLED FINGER HANG, BOTH FEET UP
scenes.narration: Here is the line, with a warning built into it. Twenty seconds of controlled, pain-free finger hang is trained territory. Forty is elite, the level of climbers who have spent years earning it. Under ten seconds, or any joint pain during the test, does not mean you are weak. It means your pulleys are not ready for this exercise yet, and readiness is a stage, not a verdict. The five mistakes in this episode share one root: they all treat the finger hang like a normal exercise that forgives enthusiasm. It does not. The pulley system is the least forgiving tissue in this entire season, and the most rewarding when respected. Hold your number, and your honesty about pain. Now the anatomy of the little rings that decide whether this exercise builds you or benches you.
scenes.sub: under 10 or any pain: build the base first - over 40: elite pulleys

lines: The tendon bows out without them.
The rings keep it gliding close.
beats.title: THE BOWSTRING PROBLEM

beats.text: A2 AND A4 DO THE HEAVY HOLDING

scenes.narration: Look at the system you are loading. Your finger tendons are powerful cables, but a cable pulling around a bend wants to straighten, to bowstring away from the bone. What stops it is a series of small ligament rings called pulleys, strapped over the tendon like the guides on a fishing rod. They hold the cable close to the finger so your pull becomes grip instead of geometry loss. Two of them, known to climbers as A2 and A4, carry most of the load. Here is the asymmetry that rules this episode: the tendon is one of the strongest tissues in your body, and the pulleys are small rings of ligament that adapt far more slowly and complain far more quietly. When climbers injure fingers, it is rarely the cable that fails. It is a ring, overloaded by a load the tendon handled easily. Every mistake that follows is a way of asking the rings to pay for the cable's strength. This is also why finger training has the strictest culture in all of strength sports. Climbers protect these rings the way singers protect their voices, because for them, the rings are the instrument.

lines: Muscle adapts in weeks. Ligament in months.
beats.title: THE ADAPTATION GAP

scenes.narration: Here is the timeline problem underneath all five mistakes. Muscle adapts in weeks. Tendon adapts in months. Ligament, the pulley tissue, adapts slowest of all, and it does so silently, without the pump or burn that tells you work is happening. So a motivated beginner's finger strength climbs on the muscle schedule, feels ready for more on the tendon schedule, and loads the pulleys on a schedule they cannot match. The gap is invisible until it is not. Climbers learned this the hard way over decades, and their culture now treats finger loading with a respect that looks almost superstitious from outside. It is not superstition. It is the adaptation gap, respected. The rule that protects everything in this episode is simple: your finger training progresses at the speed of your slowest tissue. The rings set the pace. The cable just comes along for the ride it was already strong enough for. Respect is not fear. It is simply training at the speed of the tissue you cannot afford to lose.

beats.text: THE OPEN HAND IS THE SAFE GRIP
FULL CRIMP IS THE ADVANCED EXAM
EARN THE CRIMP, NEVER START THERE

scenes.narration: One more piece of anatomy before the mistakes, because it decides which grip you are allowed to use. Finger hangs come in positions. The open hand, fingers extended and draped, loads the pulleys gently because the tendon runs relatively straight. The full crimp, thumb locked over fingers and joints hyperextended, multiplies pulley load dramatically, because the cable bends at its sharpest angle exactly where the A2 ring holds it. Climbers measure this difference in multiples, not percentages. Beginners, of course, crimp instinctively, because it feels stronger, and it is: the position borrows strength from the rings' suffering. Every protocol in this episode is open-hand only. The crimp is an advanced exam you may sit after a year of patient base work, not a starting position. If anything you have seen online taught you to crimp from day one, that advice is mistake zero, and it is the reason the other five mistakes hurt so many people.
Now hang with me, carefully. Open hand, fingers draped, ten seconds, feet ready to catch you. Smooth on, smooth off, zero pain allowed. This is how pulleys get built. Go.

beats.text: MISTAKE 1: MAX HANGS FROM DAY ONE
MISTAKE 2: FULL CRIMPING AS A BEGINNER

scenes.narration: Here are the five mistakes, in the order they usually injure people. Mistake one: maximum hangs from day one. Your muscles feel ready, so you load your full bodyweight on small fingers immediately, and the rings meet a load they needed months to prepare for. Mistake two: full crimping as a beginner, borrowing strength from the A2 pulley at multiples of the open-hand load. Mistake three: training through joint pain. A pulley that aches during a hang is filing a report; men who override it get the full letter later, as a pop and a season on the couch. Mistake four: daily finger training. The rings rebuild slower than any tissue in this series, and daily loading outruns their repair completely. Mistake five: dynamic moves, jumping to the ledge or dropping off it, which spike the load far beyond your bodyweight for an instant the rings must pay for. And the thread through all five: if you develop finger joint pain that lingers between sessions, stop the hangs and see a professional if it persists. That sentence is not legal decoration. It is the difference between a training block and an injury story.

lines: That order is the whole secret.
beats.title: YOUR VERDICT

scenes.narration: So, your readiness number. Under ten seconds, or any pain in the test: your assignment is the base, towel hangs, bar hangs, pinch work, for a month before you retest. Ten to twenty, pain-free: you may train finger hangs twice a week, open hand, feet-assisted as needed, at loads that feel almost easy. Over forty: your pulleys are genuinely earned, climber-grade, and you know exactly how long that took. Whatever your number is, it is a measurement of readiness, not a grade on you. Drop your seconds in the comments, just the number, and be honest if the test hurt, because honesty is the training variable that matters most in this episode. Retest in thirty days. The rings reward the patient and invoice the proud, every single time. Write your number down, and write the word silent or loud beside it. That one word is your real progress report.
Same ledge, open hand, thirty days from now: that is the retest. If this way of training makes sense to you, subscribe, because we test a new cable every episode. This is {channel}. Train the cable.

title: 5 finger hangs Mistakes That Are Destroying Your finger pulleys
